reason: The sources support a viable story with 15 dual-sourced claims covering Ulysses' unique trajectory, discovery facts, launch delays, and operational longevity.
story: In 1990, the joint NASA-ESA probe Ulysses launched aboard Space Shuttle Discovery on an unprecedented mission: to become the first spacecraft to explore the space above and below the Sun's poles. Direct launches into polar solar orbits were impossible with existing rockets, so planners dispatched Ulysses toward Jupiter for a gravity assist in February 1992. Jupiter's gravity bent the probe's flight path away from the ecliptic plane into an 80-degree inclination. At launch, Ulysses became the fastest human-made object ever accelerated up to that point. Along its 18-year voyage, Ulysses discovered that the Sun's polar magnetic field was much weaker than assumed, deep-space cosmic dust was 30 times more abundant than expected, and solar wind weakened to a 50-year low. Despite budget cuts that eliminated its sister craft and a 1986 delay caused by the Challenger disaster, Ulysses survived over four times its expected lifetime before operations ended on June 30, 2009.
angle: To explore the Sun's poles, Ulysses had to launch to Jupiter first, using giant planetary gravity to bend its orbit 80 degrees out of the Solar System's plane.

claims.claim: Ulysses was a joint space mission between NASA and the European Space Agency (ESA).
Ulysses was launched on October 6, 1990, aboard Space Shuttle Discovery.
Ulysses was the first spacecraft to explore and study the space environment above and below the Sun's poles.
The mission was originally planned as a two-spacecraft mission before US budget cutbacks cancelled the American probe in 1981.
The launch of Ulysses was delayed from 1986 to 1990 due to the Space Shuttle Challenger disaster.
To reach a high solar orbital inclination, Ulysses executed a gravity assist flyby of Jupiter in February 1992.
The Jupiter gravity assist bent Ulysses' trajectory into an orbit inclined at about 80 degrees to the ecliptic plane.
At the time of its launch, Ulysses achieved the highest speed of any human-made spacecraft up to that point.
NASA provided the Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (RTG) to power the spacecraft.
Ulysses unexpectedly passed through comet tails three times during its mission.
Data from Ulysses revealed that the magnetic field at the Sun's poles was much weaker than previously assumed.
Ulysses determined that interstellar dust entering the Solar System was 30 times more abundant than previously expected.
Measurements showed that the solar wind had progressively weakened, reaching its lowest level in at least 50 years.
Ulysses operated for more than 18 years, exceeding its expected design lifetime by more than four times.
Ground controllers officially ceased operations and lost final contact with Ulysses on June 30, 2009.

disputed: Planned end dates shifted: S1 notes a planned shutdown on July 1, 2008 that was extended due to workarounds, while final shutdown occurred June 30, 2009. Scripts should simply cite the final June 30, 2009 end date.
